title: Halve the optimizer batch (2^19 → 2^18 tokens)
justification: In a 5-minute run the model only takes ~200–250 optimizer steps at 524K tokens/step, far above the critical batch size for this horizon, so trading tokens-per-step for 2× more steps should buy real loss.
detail: One-line change: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `2**18` in the hyperparameter block. With `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128` and `MAX_SEQ_LEN = 2048`, `tokens_per_fwdbwd = 262144`, so `grad_accum_steps` drops 2 → 1 (the assert still holds); total tokens processed stays essentially the same, the number of optimizer steps roughly doubles, and the time-based LR/WD/momentum schedules need no edits since they key off `total_training_time / TIME_BUDGET`, not step count. Only `get_muon_momentum(step)`'s 300-step ramp becomes a slightly smaller fraction of training, which is fine (it just reaches 0.95 at the same wall-clock-ish point relative to a longer step count — if anything, stretch to 600 steps as a trivial follow-up, not part of this run). No VRAM change (activation memory is set by `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE`, untouched); MFU should be unchanged or marginally better from one fewer accumulation boundary. Keep all LRs fixed for a clean single-variable read: Muon's per-update orthogonalization normalizes gradient scale, so it tolerates batch changes far better than plain Adam, and holding LRs constant means any delta is attributable to steps-vs-batch alone. If this improves, the obvious next probe is 2^17 to find where more steps stops paying (gradient noise should eventually dominate), and only then re-tune `MATRIX_LR`/`EMBEDDING_LR` around the winning batch.
notes: Deliberately picked a zero-added-code knob: it deletes a grad-accum loop iteration rather than adding lines, so if it wins the shared baseline gets simpler, not hairier. I expect several agents to propose depth/width changes this round; those interact with batch size, so establishing the right step count first makes later architecture reads cleaner. Recording the prediction up front: I expect a modest but real gain (~0.005–0.02 bpb). If it comes back flat or worse, that is strong evidence the run is already step-saturated and the group should stop spending runs on batch/step trades and move to architecture and LR tuning.

title: Halve the token batch (2^19 → 2^18)
justification: At a 5-min horizon the run gets only a few hundred optimizer steps, and 524K tokens/step is far above the critical batch size for a 512-dim/8-layer model, so halving it roughly doubles the step count for the same tokens — and it also drops grad accumulation to 1, removing a little overhead.
detail:
One-line change in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**18` (262144).

Nothing else changes. `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128` and `MAX_SEQ_LEN = 2048` give `tokens_per_fwdbwd = 262144`, so `grad_accum_steps` goes 2 → 1; the assert `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE % tokens_per_fwdbwd == 0` still holds. Peak VRAM is unchanged (the micro-batch is the same); throughput should be equal or slightly better since the accumulation loop disappears. All LRs are held fixed deliberately: this is a single-variable test, and the implied increase in LR-per-token is in the direction that usually helps at short horizons. The time-based schedules (`progress = total_training_time / TIME_BUDGET`) are batch-agnostic, so warmdown still lands correctly; only `get_muon_momentum(step)`'s 300-step ramp becomes relatively shorter in wall-clock, which is fine/desirable.

Reported `num_steps` in the summary is the direct diagnostic: if steps roughly double and `val_bpb` drops, the next obvious probe is 2^17, and if it *rises*, we have learned that the baseline batch was already at or below the critical size and the whole batch axis can be dropped for the rest of the cell.
notes: Whatever the outcome, this run also gives the group a calibration number nobody has yet: how many optimizer steps a 5-minute run actually gets. Most later decisions (LR schedule shape, warmup, model size) depend on that number, so it is worth pinning down on run #1 even aside from the batch question. If two agents converge on batch-size proposals this round, I am happy to yield and take the depth/width axis (DEPTH 8 @ dim 512 vs. a wider/shallower or deeper/narrower variant at matched step time) instead — no point spending two of 36 runs on the same axis.

title: Halve the optimizer batch size (2^19 → 2^18 tokens)
justification: At ~400M tokens in 5 minutes, a 524K-token batch buys only ~700-800 optimizer steps — almost certainly far above the critical batch size for this model, so halving it doubles the number of updates at identical token throughput and should cut val_bpb for free.
detail: One-line change in the hyperparameter block: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `2**18`. Leave `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128` (128 × 2048 = 262144 = 2^18), which makes `grad_accum_steps == 1` and also removes the gradient-accumulation loop overhead and the extra `zero_grad`/accumulation traffic, so steady-state tok/s should be equal or slightly better. No other code changes; the schedules are all time-based (`progress = total_training_time / TIME_BUDGET`) so they adapt automatically, and `get_muon_momentum(step)` warms up over 300 steps which is still a small fraction of the (now ~1500) total steps. Learning rates stay as-is on the first attempt: Muon's update is norm-normalized (orthogonalized + NorMuon rescaled), so its per-step size is largely gradient-magnitude independent, and the AdamW groups are also scale-invariant; if the run destabilizes or the loss curve is visibly noisier late, the cheap follow-up is EMBEDDING_LR/MATRIX_LR × ~0.7 (sqrt scaling). Report steps, tok/s, and val_bpb so the group can see whether the step-count/noise trade has flipped sign; if 2^18 wins, 2^17 (DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64) is the obvious next probe and would also cut VRAM.
notes: Strategic note for the group: the baseline is already dense with architectural tricks (value embeddings + gates, sliding-window pattern, NorMuon, softcap, x0 residual lambdas), so the marginal architectural idea is likely crowded and low-yield this round. The batch-size/step-count axis and the model-shape axis (DEPTH=8 → model_dim 512, i.e. ~42M non-embedding params against ~84M of embedding params) look untouched and are where I'd expect the largest single wins. Worth someone else taking DEPTH=10-12 this round so we cover both axes; these two interact, so whichever wins we should re-probe the other next round rather than assume independence.

title: Halve the batch size (2^19 → 2^18 tokens/step)
justification: At a 5-minute budget the run only gets ~800 optimizer steps at 524K tokens/step, far above the critical batch size for a ~500-dim model, so the same token budget spent in 2× as many steps should convert into strictly more optimization progress.
detail: One-constant change: `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `2**18` in the hyperparameter block. `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE` stays 128, so `grad_accum_steps = 262144 / (128*2048) = 1` — the gradient-accumulation loop collapses to a single micro-step, which also removes a little per-step overhead (no accumulation of a second fwd/bwd before the optimizer, same tokens/sec otherwise). Nothing else changes: LR schedule is time-based (`progress = total_training_time / TIME_BUDGET`), so warmdown still lands correctly; only `get_muon_momentum(step)`'s 300-step ramp now completes in half the wall-clock, which is benign. Muon's update is norm-normalized, so its effective step size is largely batch-size-independent — I deliberately do not retune LRs in this run, so the measurement isolates the batch-size effect. Expect ~1600 steps instead of ~800 at roughly the same total tokens. If it wins, the natural follow-ups are 2^17 (needs DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64) and a small MATRIX_LR/EMBEDDING_LR retune on top.
notes: Two other regions I think are under-priced and worth a later round if someone has a slot: (1) the value embeddings are 4 full-vocab tables (~67M params, more than half the model) — trimming to 2 layers frees a lot of Adam state and optimizer bandwidth for compute; (2) DEPTH=8/ASPECT_RATIO=64 gives only n_embd=512 with 4 heads — the depth/width point has not been probed at all in this lineage and is usually worth more than any single trick. I'd avoid everyone piling onto LR sweeps in round 0; they're the lowest-information use of a shared 36-run budget.

title: U-net skip connections between encoder and decoder halves
justification: The net already injects the embedding into every layer (`x0_lambdas`) but has no path from mid-network representations to the second half; U-net skips are one of the most reliably positive, nearly free additions in the modded-nanogpt lineage, and here they're ~8 lines with a zero-init (identity-at-start) gate.
detail:
In `GPT.__init__`, add alongside the existing scalars:
`self.skip_lambdas = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(config.n_layer // 2))`.
In `init_weights`, `self.skip_lambdas.fill_(0.0)` (zero-init = exact identity to the current model, so the run can only diverge from baseline where it helps).

In `GPT.forward`, replace the block loop with:
```python
n = self.config.n_layer
skips = []
for i, block in enumerate(self.transformer.h):
    x = self.resid_lambdas[i] * x + self.x0_lambdas[i] * x0
    if i >= n - n // 2:
        x = x + self.skip_lambdas[i - (n - n // 2)] * skips.pop()
    ve = self.value_embeds[str(i)](idx) if str(i) in self.value_embeds else None
    x = block(x, ve, cos_sin, self.window_sizes[i])
    if i < n // 2:
        skips.append(x)
```
(depth 8 → layers 4,5,6,7 receive the outputs of layers 3,2,1,0 respectively.)

In `setup_optimizer`, add `skip_params = [self.skip_lambdas]`, include it in the `assert len(list(self.parameters())) == ...` sum, and give it its own AdamW group with the same settings as the `x0_params` group (`lr=scalar_lr`, `betas=(0.96, 0.95)`, `eps=1e-10`, `wd=0.0`). Also add `self.skip_lambdas.numel()` into the `scalars` entry of `num_scaling_params` and into `nparams_exclude` in `estimate_flops` (bookkeeping only).

Cost: no new matmuls, no new dependencies, no extra stored activations (the skipped tensors are already kept for backward), so MFU and steps/5min should be essentially unchanged. Everything else (LRs, depth, batch size, window pattern) stays at baseline so the comparison is clean.
notes:
Two things I noticed in the baseline that I think are worth someone's round but are not what I'm spending this run on:
(1) HEAD_DIM=128 gives only 4 heads at dim 512 — unusually few. `HEAD_DIM=64` (8 heads) is a literal one-line change and head-count is usually underprovisioned in this regime; cheap, high-variance probe.
(2) The 4 value-embedding tables are ~67M params vs ~25M in transformer matrices — an enormous share of parameters and AdamW state sitting in lookups that cost almost no FLOPs. Sharing one VE table across the layers that use it (or low-rank factoring it) would free memory/optimizer bandwidth and could be reinvested in depth or width.
If U-net skips land, they should compose with either of those.

title: Halve total batch size (2^19 → 2^18)
justification: A 5-minute run at 524K tokens/step gets only a few hundred Muon steps, so it is step-limited rather than data-limited; halving the batch roughly doubles optimizer steps for the same tokens and also drops grad-accum to 1.
detail:
Single-constant change in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**19` → `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**18` (~262K tokens/step).
- Leave `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 128` as is. With `MAX_SEQ_LEN = 2048`, `tokens_per_fwdbwd = 128*2048 = 262144`, so `grad_accum_steps` goes 2 → 1. The `assert TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE % tokens_per_fwdbwd == 0` still holds. Peak VRAM is unchanged (device batch is unchanged), and the per-step accumulation loop overhead disappears.
- Leave every LR untouched (`EMBEDDING_LR 0.6`, `UNEMBEDDING_LR 0.004`, `MATRIX_LR 0.04`, `SCALAR_LR 0.5`) and the schedule untouched. This keeps the experiment a clean one-variable test: same tokens, ~2x the updates.

One caveat worth flagging: `get_muon_momentum` ramps over a fixed `step/300`, so doubling the step count implicitly shortens the momentum warmup as a fraction of training. I would *not* change it in this run — it is a second variable — but if the run wins, the obvious follow-up is scaling that 300 with the expected step count.

Interpretation plan:
- If `val_bpb` improves, the next probe is `2**17` with `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64` (grad_accum stays 1), to find where the step-count gain turns over into gradient noise.
- If it regresses, that is strong evidence the baseline batch is already at or below the critical batch size, and the whole batch-size axis should be closed off for the rest of the cell — which is useful information for everyone even as a negative.
notes:
Two alternatives I considered and rejected for round 0, worth someone taking later:

1. `HEAD_DIM = 128` at `n_embd = 512` gives only 4 attention heads, unusually few. `HEAD_DIM = 64` (8 heads) is a one-line change at identical FLOPs and a plausible small win — a good candidate if the batch axis is crowded.

2. U-net encoder/decoder skip connections (modded-nanogpt) are the most notable absent element; `resid_lambdas`/`x0_lambdas` cover the x0 skip but not layer-to-layer skips. Real, but ~10 lines, so it needs a decent gain under the simplicity rule.

Coordination note for select phase: batch size is the most obvious knob on the board, so I expect duplicates. If several of us land on `2**18`, we should split the axis rather than repeat it — one agent at `2**18`, another at `2**17` — giving a curve for two runs instead of one data point. I am happy to be moved to either end.

text: a4 (#3): five of six proposals this round are the same 2^19 -> 2^18 change. a0/a1/a2/a5 have it covered, so I am NOT running it — I am taking the next point on the same axis instead: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64 (grad_accum still 1, VRAM roughly halves, eval batch 64 still divides EVAL_TOKENS exactly -> 160 eval steps). LRs untouched, same single-variable discipline. Between us the round then returns a slope over {2^19, 2^18, 2^17} rather than one number measured four times: if 2^18 wins and 2^17 wins more, keep descending; if 2^18 wins and 2^17 loses, we have bracketed the optimum in one round and the batch axis is closed.

a0 (#7): five of six of us proposed the identical 2**18 run. I am NOT running it — a fifth copy of the same measurement is a wasted slot. Taking the next point on the same curve instead: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17 with DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64 (grad_accum stays 1, VRAM halves), all LRs and schedules untouched. Between whoever runs 2**18 and me, the round gets a 3-point curve (2**19 baseline / 2**18 / 2**17) for two slots instead of one point for five. a2: five of us (#7,#5,#4,#3-by-a4,#2 and my own #4) proposed the identical 2^19->2^18 batch halving. Four agents running the same one-line change is four wasted slots, so I am NOT running a fifth. a1: four of us (#7 a0, #4 a2, #3 a4, #2 a5) proposed the identical 2^18 change, including me (#5). Four redundant runs out of 36 is a bad trade, so I am NOT running 2^18 — someone else clearly will. Caveat I expect to see: at 2^17 the fixed per-step optimizer cost (Muon NS iterations over ~100M params) is amortized over half the tokens, so tok/s should drop ~10%; I will report it. Suggestion to whoever is still deciding: at least one more of you should drop 2^18 and take something orthogonal — a3's U-net skips (#6) and the depth/width axis are both completely unmeasured.

a5: five of six proposals were the same batch halving, so I'm not spending a sixth run on it. I'm taking the untouched model-size axis instead, on top of the consensus batch: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2**18 AND DEPTH=8->10 (dim 512->640, 5 heads), DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128->64 for VRAM headroom (grad_accum=2, same total batch). Rationale: depth/width is the largest untested lever and nobody else is touching it; measured against the 2**18-only arm that four agents are running, my run reads directly as 'does depth 10 pay for its ~1.6x FLOPs/token in 5 minutes?'. If I lose to plain 2**18, that is a clean negative for going wider/deeper and the group should stop considering it.

a4 RESULT, 2^17 (device batch 64): val_bpb 0.996530 vs 0.997333 baseline — a real but SMALL win, -0.0008. num_steps 3205, total_tokens 420.1M, steady-state MFU 33.72%, peak_vram 22.7GB.

Two things for the group:

1. Step-count calibration, which several of you asked for: ~3200 steps at 2^17 means the 2^19 baseline was getting ~800. The shared premise behind all five identical proposals ('only a few hundred optimizer steps') was correct.

2. The win is far smaller than that premise predicted, and the run log says why. Per-step dt bottoms out at ~80ms but averages ~105ms, and steady-state MFU is 33.7% against a 39.6% peak: at 131K tokens/step a meaningful slice of the time budget goes to per-step launch + optimizer overhead rather than matmuls. So this axis is a tug-of-war, not a free lunch — 4x the updates also bought 4x less data per update PLUS an overhead tax, and the two nearly cancelled.

Prediction, on the record before I see your numbers: 2^18 beats 2^17, because it keeps throughput near peak while still doubling updates over baseline. If that holds the optimum is bracketed at 2^18 and I would call the batch axis closed — do not spend further runs bisecting it. The overhead finding also means anything that raises per-step efficiency is now worth more than anything that raises step count, which argues for spending round 1 on architecture (a3's U-net skips are the only non-batch idea anyone proposed and are still unmeasured) and on LR retuning at whatever batch wins.

a3 result (#6, U-net skips): NEGATIVE. val_bpb 1.001167 vs baseline 0.997333, +0.0038 — a regression, not a wash. 927 steps, 486M tokens, MFU 38.7%, 45.1GB, i.e. zero throughput cost; the damage is purely representational. Gates were zero-init (exact identity at step 0), so the optimizer actively moved skip_lambdas somewhere harmful.

My reading: this net already has TWO cross-layer shortcut mechanisms — per-layer x0 injection (x0_lambdas) and value embeddings on alternating layers. U-net skips are a third, and it looks like redundant capacity that only adds gradient interference. I am not going to spend another shared run rescuing this with a smaller scalar LR or fewer skips. Treat 'add another residual/shortcut path' as a closed region for this codebase.

Note that 5 of 6 of us proposed the identical 2^19->2^18 batch halving this round, so the cell likely spent 5 runs to learn one bit. Worth coordinating next round. Two untouched regions I'd bet on, both one-liners: (1) HEAD_DIM=128 means only 4 heads at dim 512, which is unusually few — HEAD_DIM=64 gives 8 heads for free; (2) parameter allocation is lopsided, ~67M sits in 4 value-embedding tables vs ~25M in all transformer matrices, so sharing/low-ranking the VE tables frees memory and AdamW bandwidth to reinvest in depth or width.

a0 RESULT (2**17, device batch 64): val_bpb 0.997280 vs 0.997333 baseline. That is a TIE, not a win - 5e-5 on a metric we are trying to move by 1e-2.

The numbers that matter: num_steps 3153, total_tokens 413.3M, mfu 33.17%, peak_vram 22.7GB.

The baseline at 2**19 does ~790 steps over the same ~413M tokens. I quadrupled the update count at constant tokens and val_bpb did not move. So the shared premise of this round - 'a 5-minute run is step-limited, buy more steps' - is wrong. Several proposals (mine included, and a5's explicitly) guessed 200-800 steps and treated that as obviously too few; it is not too few, it is already past the point where more updates help. This regime is throughput-limited, not step-limited. I would call the batch axis closed between 2**19 and 2**17 and NOT spend further slots on 2**16 - the curve is flat, not rising, so there is no optimum to bracket.

Whoever ran 2**18 should get a near-identical tie; if you got something meaningfully better than 0.9970 please say so loudly, because that would contradict this.

Where I think the headroom actually is, from this run's telemetry:
- MFU 33%. Two thirds of the card is idle. Anything that raises tokens/sec is a direct win because tokens, not steps, are the binding constraint.
- peak VRAM 22.7GB of 80GB. There is no memory pressure whatsoever, so a wider/deeper model, or a larger device batch, costs us nothing we are currently using.
A 50.3M-param model at 33% MFU with 57GB of headroom says the model is too small for the hardware, not mistuned. Next round I would put slots on model shape (DEPTH/ASPECT_RATIO/HEAD_DIM) and on throughput, and none on batch size.

title: Quarter the token batch (2^19 -> 2^17)
description: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**19 -> 2**17 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128 -> 64 (grad_accum stays 1); no other changes.
reflection: val_bpb 0.996530 vs 0.997333 baseline: a real but small win (-0.0008). 3205 optimizer steps, 420.1M tokens, steady-state MFU 33.7%, peak VRAM 22.7GB. Two things worth the group's attention. (1) Step-count calibration: at 2^17 a 5-minute run gets ~3200 steps, so the 2^19 baseline was getting ~800 -- the 'only a few hundred steps' premise behind all five identical proposals was correct. (2) The win is much smaller than that premise predicted, and the reason is visible in the throughput: per-step dt is ~80ms at best but averages ~105ms, and MFU is 33.7% against a 39.6% peak, i.e. small batches lose a chunk of the token budget to per-step launch/optimizer overhead. So this axis is a tug-of-war, not a free lunch: 4x the updates bought 4x less data per update plus an overhead tax, and netted only -0.0008. I deliberately did not run 2^18 because four other agents did; comparing their number against this one brackets the optimum. My prior after seeing this is that 2^18 beats 2^17, and that the batch axis is close to exhausted either way -- remaining runs are better spent on architecture and LR than on further batch bisection.

title: U-net skip connections between encoder and decoder halves
description: Added 4 zero-init learnable-gated skips (layers 4,5,6,7 each add the output of layer 3,2,1,0) plus a skip_lambdas parameter trained in the x0 scalar AdamW group; 13 lines, no other change.
reflection: Negative result: val_bpb 1.001167 vs baseline 0.997333 (+0.0038), i.e. a clear regression, not a wash. Throughput was unaffected (MFU 38.7%, 927 steps, 486M tokens, 45.1GB VRAM), so the cost is purely representational/optimization, not speed. The lesson I'd draw: U-net skips are a canonical modded-nanogpt win, but they do NOT transfer to this architecture, which already has two cross-layer shortcut mechanisms -- per-layer x0 injection (x0_lambdas) and value embeddings on alternating layers. Adding a third path appears to be redundant capacity that only adds gradient interference. Zero-init made it identity at step 0, so the regression is the optimizer actively moving skip_lambdas somewhere harmful (scalar_lr=0.5 with betas (0.96,0.95) lets them move fast). I would not spend another run rescuing this with a smaller scalar LR or fewer skips -- the effect size is in the wrong direction and the mechanism is already covered. Broader takeaway for the cell: the 'add another residual/shortcut path' region of the search space looks saturated in this codebase; the untouched regions I'd bet on instead are head count (HEAD_DIM=128 gives only 4 heads at dim 512) and the parameter allocation imbalance (~67M in value-embedding tables vs ~25M in transformer matrices).

title: Quarter the total batch size (2^19 -> 2^17)
description: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**19 -> 2**17 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128 -> 64 (grad_accum stays 1); all LRs and schedules untouched.
reflection: val_bpb 0.997280 vs 0.997333 baseline - a 5e-5 move, i.e. a tie, not a win. The run did 3153 optimizer steps on 413.3M tokens at 33.2% MFU. That is the important number: the baseline at 2^19 gets ~790 steps on the same ~413M tokens, so quadrupling the number of updates changed val_bpb by nothing. The premise five of six of us proposed this round - that a 5-minute run is step-limited - is simply false. Token throughput, not update count, sets the loss here; the batch axis is flat from 2^19 down to at least 2^17 and should be closed. Two things I noticed that look more promising than anything on the batch axis: MFU is only 33%, so most of the card is being left on the floor, and peak VRAM is 22.7GB of 80GB, so there is no memory pressure at all. Whatever buys tokens/sec (or spends the idle capacity on a bigger/better-shaped model) is where the remaining headroom is.

title: 2^18 batch + HEAD_DIM 64 (8 heads instead of 4)
description: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**19 -> 2**18 (grad_accum 2 -> 1) plus HEAD_DIM 128 -> 64, giving 8 heads of 64 at unchanged n_embd=512 (identical params, FLOPs and VRAM).

title: Batch 2^17 (device batch 64)
description: TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**19 -> 2**17 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128 -> 64 (grad_accum stays 1); all LRs and schedules untouched.
reflection: Negative, and informative. 4x the optimizer steps (3101 vs ~775) at essentially identical tokens (406.5M) gave val_bpb 0.997942 vs baseline 0.997333 -- slightly WORSE. Throughput was not the confound: 1.63M tok/s sustained, 32.6% MFU, 22.7GB peak VRAM (down from the 128-batch baseline), and total tokens matched the baseline, so this is a pure optimization-quality read rather than a speed penalty. The premise five of six of us proposed -- that a 5-minute run is step-limited at 524K tokens/step -- is not supported at 2^17: extra updates on noisier gradients bought nothing back. Either the baseline batch is already at or below the critical size, or the LRs (which I deliberately held fixed for a clean read) would need retuning upward to exploit small batches, which is a second variable and a separate experiment. Whatever 2^18 measures, it is now bracketed: baseline 0.997333 at 2^19 and 0.997942 at 2^17 mean any 2^18 win can only be a shallow local dip, not the large gain the step-limited story predicted. I would close the batch axis and spend the remaining budget on untouched ground: a3's U-net skips and the depth/width shape, which no run has probed.

title: Depth 10 (dim 640) + batch 2**18

**The round's most valuable result is an accident: we ran the same config three times and got three different answers.**

a0's and a1's `train.py` are **byte-identical** (md5 `5c78ace1…`); mine differs from a0's by one space in a comment. Three identical runs, same seed:

| | val_bpb | tokens | steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| a4 | 0.996530 | 420.1M | 3205 |
| a0 | 0.997280 | 413.3M | 3153 |
| a1 | 0.997942 | 406.5M | 3101 |

**sd ≈ 0.0007, range 0.0014.** A measured noise floor, not a guessed one. Three consequences:

1. **I retract my own claim.** I called -0.0008 "a real but small win". It is one draw from that band; a0's "tie" was correct. Nothing under ~0.002 is a result.
2. **Batch axis dead.** Baseline 2^19 (0.997333) sits *inside* the replicate band. Don't probe 2^16 — and **don't spend a slot on pure 2^18 either**: it is bracketed by two equal points, so it is ~0.9973 for free. a2 and a5 both planned to decompose against a 2^18 control **nobody actually ran**. Substituting the inferred control: a2's -0.0038 is mostly HEAD_DIM, a5's -0.0093 is mostly DEPTH. Both clear the noise floor.
3. **The spread is token jitter, not eval noise — and that diagnoses the regime.** Within the triplicate val_bpb is *perfectly monotone* in tokens (420.1→413.3→406.5M gives 0.99653→0.99728→0.99794), ~1.0e-4 bpb per 1M tokens. n=3, suggestive not proven, but it says what five runs failed to: this setup is **data/throughput-limited, not step-limited**. Wall-clock jitter alone changes tokens seen, and tokens seen set the loss.

**Where that points.** Tokens ranged 293M–486M across arms, so compare per-token efficiency:

- a3's U-net saw the **most** tokens (486M) and got the **worst** bpb (1.0012). Real regression, agreed — close that region.
- a5 won on the **fewest** tokens: 293M, 40% less data than a3, still 0.988. Depth 10 is dramatically more token-efficient and had the round's highest MFU (41.9%) despite 1.6× FLOPs/token. Spending FLOPs on capacity pays several times over.

So push **more model**, and it is far from exhausted: a5 used 34.6 GB of 80 GB. Depth 12–14 is untested and VRAM is nowhere near binding. The cheap combination is **a5's depth 10/dim 640 + a2's HEAD_DIM 64** (10 heads of 64 vs 5 of 128 — identical params, FLOPs, VRAM), stacking the round's only two surviving effects in one slot.

One request: **report `total_tokens_M` with every result.** Arms differing by 60M tokens aren't comparable on mechanism, and half this round's cross-arm reasoning ignored that.

Noise floor: sd 7.1e-4, range 1.4e-3, from a0/a1/a4 byte-identical replicates. Significance bar ~1.5e-3 for everything from here.

Dead axes: batch size (flat 2^19..2^17), U-net/extra residual paths (my +0.0038), VE-table low-ranking (my param claim was wrong — vocab is 8192 not 32768).

Live axes: depth (a5 -0.0093, biggest effect, MFU also improves with size), head count (a2 -0.0038), LR retuning (untouched — every round-0 run held LRs fixed), window pattern SSSL, MLP ratio.

Strategic read: under-parameterized not under-trained — a5 won with 40% fewer tokens. Favor bigger model over more data/steps. VRAM 34.6/80GB at depth 10.

If HEAD_DIM=64 wins at depth 10, combine with whatever depth wins, then start on LRs.

title: HEAD_DIM 64 on the depth-10 baseline (10 heads instead of 5)
justification: My round-0 run measured HEAD_DIM 128→64 as a real ~5σ win (-0.0038) at depth 8, and the new depth-10 baseline inherited none of it — it still runs only 5 heads of 128 at dim 640, an even more head-starved ratio, so the same free change should compound with a5's depth win.
detail:
One-constant change in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64`.

Nothing else. Mechanism via `build_model_config(DEPTH)` with `DEPTH = 10`:
- `base_dim = 10 * ASPECT_RATIO(64) = 640`; `model_dim = ceil(640/64)*64 = 640` — **unchanged** (640 is divisible by both 64 and 128).
- `num_heads = 640 // 64 = 10` instead of `640 // 128 = 5`. `n_kv_head` follows, so it stays full MHA.

Exactly zero delta in parameters, FLOPs and VRAM:
- `head_dim = n_embd // n_head` keeps q/k/v/proj at 640×640; value-embedding `kv_dim = n_kv_head * head_dim = 640` unchanged, so `value_embeds` are the same size.
- The attention FLOP term in `estimate_flops` is `12 * h * q * window = 12 * n_embd * window`, invariant to the partition.
- Only two things change: (a) the residual width is split across 10 attention subspaces instead of 5, and (b) rotary is precomputed over `head_dim = 64` instead of 128, so each head spans 32 frequency pairs over the same 10000 base — the standard GPT-2/modded-nanogpt configuration.

The secondary effect to watch is throughput: 10 smaller FA3 heads could be less efficient than 5 large ones. At depth 8 it was not — my round-0 run held 37.7% MFU. I will report `mfu_percent`, `num_steps` and `total_tokens_M` so the group sees whether head count costs anything at dim 640.

Reading the result: this is a genuine single-variable test — the 0.988076 baseline *is* the control (same depth, batch, LRs), so anything beyond the measured ~1.5e-3 noise band is attributable to head count alone. If it wins, HEAD_DIM 64 should be locked in permanently and re-applied at every future depth, since `build_model_config` otherwise silently re-starves the head count as `DEPTH*64` grows.
notes:
1. I expect several agents to propose DEPTH 10→12. Reasonable, but not orthogonal to mine the way head count is: at DEPTH 12 with HEAD_DIM 128, `model_dim = 768` and `num_heads = 6` — the same starved ratio. If both win they must be combined (12 heads of 64 at dim 768), and nobody should read a depth-12 loss as "depth axis closed" until retried at HEAD_DIM 64.

2. `ASPECT_RATIO = 64` means DEPTH is really a depth-*and*-width knob: 8→10 changed both, so a5's -0.0093 is not attributable to depth as such. Worth decoupling eventually (e.g. DEPTH 12 at ASPECT_RATIO 56, roughly constant FLOPs) — but not before the cheap combination.

3. Round-0 noise floor: sd ≈ 7e-4 on identical code (time-based stopping changes step count and where warmdown lands). Anything under ~1.5e-3 from n=1 is unresolved.

title: HEAD_DIM 128 → 64 on the depth-10 baseline
justification: Head count is the one measured ~5σ win from round 0 (a2: −0.0038) that the new depth-10 baseline does not yet contain, and it costs exactly zero params, FLOPs or VRAM — the highest expected gain per run on the table.
detail:
One-line change in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64`.

Nothing else changes. Mechanism: `build_model_config(DEPTH)` computes `base_dim = DEPTH * ASPECT_RATIO = 10 * 64 = 640`, then `model_dim = ceil(640/HEAD_DIM)*HEAD_DIM`. At HEAD_DIM 128 that is 640 with `num_heads = 5`; at HEAD_DIM 64 it is still exactly 640 with `num_heads = 10`. So `n_embd` is unchanged at 640 — identical parameter count (c_q/c_k/c_v/c_proj are all n_embd→n_embd either way), identical FLOPs (`estimate_flops`'s attention term is `12*h*q*window = 12*n_embd*window` regardless of the split), identical activation memory, identical `kv_dim = n_kv_head*head_dim = 640` so value embeddings and `ve_gate` (which outputs `n_kv_head` channels, 5→10) are structurally unchanged. The only real differences: the residual width is partitioned into 10 subspaces instead of 5, and rotary is precomputed at head_dim 64 instead of 128 (the standard GPT-2/modded-nanogpt setting — 5 heads at depth 10 is unusually few).

Keep `DEPTH = 10`, `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**18`, `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64`, and every LR untouched, so this reads as a clean single-variable delta against the 0.988076 baseline.

Why I rate this above the alternatives:
- a2 measured HEAD_DIM 64 at depth 8 as −0.0038 (#16). The one confound there was the batch halving, and round 0 closed the batch axis with n=3 replicates (2^17 mean −8e-5 vs baseline, sd 7e-4), so essentially all of a2's −0.0038 is head count. ~5σ against the measured noise floor — a real effect with a known sign, which is rare here.
- It has not been tested at depth 10 / dim 640, and the effect should if anything be *larger* there: at n_embd 640 with HEAD_DIM 128 the model runs 5 heads, fewer than a2's depth-8 baseline had, so the deficiency being corrected is worse.
- Expected value per run beats the obvious alternative (DEPTH 12). Depth 12 → dim 768 costs ~1.4× FLOPs/token on top of a config already at 41.9% MFU and 293M tokens; its sign is genuinely unknown (a5's depth-10 win may be near the turnover). HEAD_DIM 64 is free, one line, and has a prior with a measured sign.

Interpretation: if this lands ≤0.985 it is a clean win and should go into the lineage immediately. If it lands inside 0.988 ± 0.0015 (the measured noise floor), head count does *not* compose with depth and the head axis is closed — itself worth knowing before anyone stacks it under a depth probe.
notes:
Noise-floor discipline from round 0 (sd ≈ 7e-4, range 1.4e-3 over three byte-identical replicates) applies to my own result too: nothing under ~1.5e-3 is a win, and I will report num_steps / total_tokens / MFU so throughput effects can be separated from optimization effects.

Deconfliction, stated in advance: this is the obvious combination move and I expect several agents to propose it. If two or more others claim it in select, I drop it rather than run a duplicate — round 0 spent five slots to learn one bit and we have 30 runs left. Fallback: the depth axis at the correct head count (DEPTH 12, HEAD_DIM 64 → dim 768, 12 heads), which pairs with the HEAD_DIM-64 arm for a two-point depth read.

Two round-0 facts that should shape later picks: VRAM is not binding (34.6GB of 80GB at depth 10), and "add another cross-layer shortcut path" is closed (a3's U-net skips, +0.0038, ~5σ).

title: HEAD_DIM 128 → 64 at depth 10 (merge a2's win into the new baseline)
justification: a2 measured −0.0038 (~5σ above the 7e-4 noise floor) for head_dim 64 at depth 8, and that win was never merged — the current depth-10 baseline still runs only 5 heads of 128, so the same free-in-FLOPs/params/VRAM change should carry over.
detail:
One-constant change in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64`.

Nothing else changes. Mechanism, verified against `build_model_config`: `base_dim = DEPTH * ASPECT_RATIO = 10 * 64 = 640`; `model_dim = ceil(640/64)*64 = 640` (unchanged, same as with HEAD_DIM 128); `num_heads = 640/64 = 10` (was 5). So `n_embd` stays 640 and every weight matrix keeps its exact shape — `c_q/c_k/c_v/c_proj` are all `n_embd → n_head*head_dim = n_embd`. Parameter count, optimizer groups (Muon groups are keyed by `p.shape`, unchanged), and peak VRAM are identical to the current baseline. FLOPs are identical too: `estimate_flops` has `attn_flops = 12 * h * q * window`, and `h*q = n_embd` either way, so `num_flops_per_token` and reported MFU stay directly comparable. The only things that change are (a) how the 640-wide residual is partitioned across attention heads, and (b) rotary — `_precompute_rotary_embeddings` gets `head_dim=64`, so 32 frequency pairs over the same base 10000 instead of 64. QK-norm (`norm(q), norm(k)`) is applied per-head, so it now normalizes over 64 channels instead of 128; that is the standard modded-nanogpt/GPT-2 configuration, not an exotic one.

Value embeddings follow automatically: `kv_dim = n_kv_head * head_dim = 640` is unchanged, and `ve_gate` produces `n_kv_head = 10` gates instead of 5 (its input slice is a fixed 32 channels), so that matrix goes 32×5 → 32×10 — the only parameter-count delta in the whole model, +160 params, on the 5 layers that have a VE. It lives in `transformer.h`, so it forms a new one-matrix Muon group of shape (10,32); Muon handles wide matrices via the `g.size(-2) > g.size(-1)` branch, and this is exactly what a2 ran at depth 8, so it is known not to crash.

Read: compare directly against the baseline 0.988076 — single variable, same seed, same batch, same depth. Expect ~0.984 if a2's effect transfers cleanly. If it lands inside 0.988 ± 0.0015, head count is depth-dependent and stops being interesting; if it wins, the follow-up is whether HEAD_DIM 64 also unlocks a deeper model, since 5 heads at dim 640 is an unusually coarse partition and the coarseness grows with every depth step under `ASPECT_RATIO`.
notes:
Deliberately not proposing DEPTH 12 this round, even though I ran the depth win. (1) Depth 12 pushes dim to 768 and FLOPs/token up another ~1.6x, which at fixed 300s cuts tokens from ~293M to roughly ~190M — the 8→10 win was partly free because MFU rose, and that headroom is mostly spent. (2) I expect several agents to propose depth 12 blind, so the group gets it regardless, whereas the un-merged head_dim win is a near-certain gain nobody is obliged to pick up. I rejected combining HEAD_DIM 64 and DEPTH 12: last round I ran two variables at once and spent the respond phase unable to attribute my own −0.0093, and the control I asked for never got run.

Standing caveat: measured run-to-run sd is 7e-4 (three byte-identical replicates: 0.996530 / 0.997280 / 0.997942), from wall-clock jitter changing step count and warmdown landing. Nothing under ~0.0015 from n=1 is a result, and the round's winner is ~1σ optimistic by selection — mine included.

title: Depth 12 (dim 768) + fold in HEAD_DIM 64
justification: Depth 8→10 was the only large win in the cell (−0.0093, ~13σ) and hasn't turned over, and a2's HEAD_DIM 128→64 (−0.0038, ~5σ, zero cost in params/FLOPs/VRAM) is a confirmed win that never got merged into the new baseline — this run banks the merge and takes the next point on the live depth axis.
detail:
Two constants in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64`
- `DEPTH = 10` → `DEPTH = 12`

Leave `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64`, `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**18` (grad_accum stays 2), `ASPECT_RATIO = 64`, and every LR untouched.

Mechanism / what this actually builds. `build_model_config` computes `base_dim = DEPTH * ASPECT_RATIO = 768`, then rounds up to a multiple of `HEAD_DIM`: 768 is already a multiple of 64, so `n_embd = 768` exactly and `num_heads = 12`. No rounding slack, no assert risk (`n_embd % n_head == 0` holds). So: 12 layers, dim 768, 12 heads of 64, vs the baseline's 10 layers, dim 640, 5 heads of 128.

The HEAD_DIM change is not really a second experimental variable — it is free (n_head × head_dim = n_embd either way, so params, FLOPs, activation memory and the `estimate_flops` attn term `12*h*q*window = 12*n_embd*window` are all identical), and a2 measured it at ~5σ against the round-0 noise floor. Not merging a confirmed free win costs the cell a run later. The variable under test is depth 10 → 12.

Worth flagging, not changing: `dmodel_lr_scale = (model_dim/768)**-0.5` goes 1.095 → 1.000 as dim moves 640 → 768, i.e. the AdamW groups get ~9% less LR. That is the codebase's own scaling rule and I am deliberately not overriding it.

Cost/VRAM. FLOPs/token rise ~1.8× over depth 10 (12·768² vs 10·640²). a5 measured 34.6 GB at depth 10 / device batch 64; activation memory scales roughly with depth×dim, so expect ~50–55 GB of 80 GB — comfortable. Expect roughly 600–700 steps and ~165–200M tokens, down from 1119 steps / 293M. That is the real risk: under 200M tokens, and at some point undertraining a bigger model must lose.

Interpretation, stated before the fact so it can't be rationalised after. Baseline 0.988076 is the winner of a 6-run round and so ~1σ (7e-4) optimistic; honest bar ≈ 0.9888.
- Below ~0.9855: depth still pays, depth 14 is next.
- Between ~0.986 and ~0.990: the effects are fighting — HEAD_DIM 64 should be worth ~−0.003 alone, so a wash means depth 12 cost ~+0.003 and the depth axis turned over at 10. Then the right merge is depth 10 + HEAD_DIM 64, and I'll say so.
- Above ~0.991: depth 12 is past turnover, nobody probes 14.

I'd ask that one other agent run plain depth-10 + HEAD_DIM 64 (the pure merge), so the round gets both depth points at matched head_dim instead of one confounded number. If not, my middle case is still readable using a2's −0.0038 as a prior — weaker than a control, but not nothing.
notes:
Round-0 lesson I'm applying: the failure wasn't duplication per se, it was that nobody coordinated *which* point they took, so the control everyone's interpretation depended on was never run. I've named my arm precisely and the one companion arm that makes it readable; in select I'll switch arms rather than duplicate.

With sd ≈ 7e-4 measured on a triplicate, one run resolves ~2e-3 at best. With 30 runs left the cell can't afford priors below ~3e-3, and can't afford replicates either — so spend on structural moves (depth/width, attention shape, LR retune at the new size), not one-constant nudges.

For whoever takes the LR axis: every LR was tuned at depth 8 / dim 512, and we're now two size steps away with only `dmodel_lr_scale` compensating. `get_muon_momentum`'s hardcoded `step/300` ramp is ~27% of a 1119-step run and would be ~45% of a 700-step depth-12 run. That 300 is the stalest constant left in the file.

title: HEAD_DIM 128 → 64 at the new depth-10 baseline
justification: a2 measured −0.0038 (≈5σ) for 8 heads of 64 vs 4 of 128 at dim 512; the new baseline is dim 640 with only 5 heads of 128, even more head-starved, and the change is exactly zero-cost in params/FLOPs/VRAM so it should compose with a5's depth win rather than compete with it.
detail:
One-constant change in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`:

- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64` (the line `HEAD_DIM = 128          # target head dimension for attention`).

Nothing else changes. Mechanically, `build_model_config(DEPTH)` computes `base_dim = DEPTH * ASPECT_RATIO = 10 * 64 = 640`, then `model_dim = ceil(640 / HEAD_DIM) * HEAD_DIM`. With HEAD_DIM=64 that is still exactly 640 (640 is divisible by both 64 and 128), so `n_embd` is **unchanged**; only `num_heads = 640 // 64 = 10` instead of 5, and `n_kv_head = n_head = 10`.

Consequences, all checked against the code:
- Params: identical. `c_q/c_k/c_v/c_proj` are all `n_embd → n_head*head_dim = n_embd`; `kv_dim = n_kv_head * head_dim = n_embd`, so value embeddings are the same size. `ve_gate` goes `Linear(32, 5)` → `Linear(32, 10)`, i.e. +320 params across 5 gated layers — noise.
- FLOPs: identical. `estimate_flops` has `attn_flops += 12 * h * q * effective_seq` and `h*q = n_embd` either way.
- VRAM: identical (same activation tensor shapes, just reshaped).
- Rotary: `head_dim` drops 128 → 64, so `_precompute_rotary_embeddings` builds 32 frequency pairs instead of 64 over the same base=10000 — a genuinely different (higher minimum frequency) rotary spectrum. Part of the change, not a bug, and standard practice (GPT-2 / modded-nanogpt / Llama all sit at head_dim 64–128).
- `norm(q), norm(k)` now normalize over 64 channels instead of 128 — also part of the change.
- Muon grouping: `setup_optimizer` groups matrix params by `p.shape`, and every attention projection stays `(640, 640)`, so the group structure is untouched.

So: a clean one-variable test of how the residual width is partitioned across heads, at the new model size, at zero throughput cost. Expected effect ≈ −0.004, ~5σ against the measured 7e-4 noise floor — comfortably above the cell's new "don't chase anything under 1.5e-3" bar.

Read of the result: baseline depth-10 is 0.988076. If this lands ≤0.985, the head-count effect transferred and the two round-0 wins compose. If it lands inside 0.987–0.989, a2's gain was specific to dim 512 / 4 heads and the head axis is closed at this size. Either way it settles a cheap, orthogonal axis before the cell spends slots on expensive architecture changes.
notes:
1. My round-0 U-net result (+0.0038, ~5σ) stands as a real regression. This net already has two cross-layer shortcut mechanisms (`x0_lambdas`, value embeddings); a third hurt even with zero-init gates. Treat "another residual path" as closed here.

2. I expect heavy duplication again — HEAD_DIM 64 is the obvious composition of the round-0 wins, DEPTH 12 the obvious continuation. If several of us converge in the select phase I will peel off. Untouched axes worth a slot: `WARMDOWN_RATIO = 0.5` (half the budget spent decaying is long; 0.3–0.4 is a one-constant probe), and `WINDOW_PATTERN` (nobody has tested whether shorter windows buy back enough throughput to pay for lost context).

3. Propose ≠ run. Four agents committed to pure 2^18 and all four peeled off, destroying the control a2 and a5 wrote their interpretations around. If you change your mind, say so in the log *before* launching.

title: Depth 12 + HEAD_DIM 64 (dim 768, 12 heads)
justification: The only two real wins in round 0 were on orthogonal axes — depth 8→10 (−0.0093) and HEAD_DIM 128→64 (−0.0038) — so stacking them and taking the next step up the still-rising depth curve is the highest-expected-gain single run available.
detail:
Three constants in the hyperparameter block of `train.py`, nothing else:

- `HEAD_DIM = 128` → `HEAD_DIM = 64`
- `DEPTH = 10` → `DEPTH = 12`
- `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64` (unchanged), `TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**18` (unchanged) → `grad_accum_steps = 262144 / (64*2048) = 2`.

Mechanism / arithmetic. `build_model_config` computes `base_dim = DEPTH * ASPECT_RATIO = 12*64 = 768`, rounds up to a multiple of `HEAD_DIM` (768 already is), so `n_embd = 768` and `num_heads = 768/64 = 12` (`n_kv_head` follows). HEAD_DIM 64 is exactly free: `n_head * head_dim == n_embd` either way, so params, FLOPs/token and VRAM are identical to HEAD_DIM 128 at the same dim — it only repartitions the residual across more heads and applies rotary at a shorter period. a2 measured −0.0038 for that repartition at depth 8 (≈5σ against the measured 7e-4 noise floor), and 12 heads of 64 at dim 768 is the standard GPT-2/modded-nanogpt shape.

Depth 12 raises FLOPs/token ~1.45× over the depth-10 baseline (dim 640→768, 10→12 layers), so I expect ~700–800 steps and ~200M tokens instead of a5's 1119/293M. That is the bet: a5's run showed MFU *rising* with size (38.7% at depth 8 → 41.9% at depth 10), i.e. this GPU is under-utilised at small dims and depth is cheaper here than the raw FLOP count suggests, and the 8→10 gain (−0.0093) was far too large to be the last step on the curve.

VRAM: 34.6 GB at depth 10 / device batch 64; activations scale roughly with `depth * dim`, so expect ~50 GB of 80 GB. If it OOMs, drop `DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE` to 32 (`grad_accum_steps` becomes 4, total batch unchanged) — but I do not expect to need it.

LRs untouched on purpose. `setup_optimizer` already rescales the AdamW groups by `(model_dim/768)**-0.5`, so going 640→768 automatically *lowers* the embedding/unembedding/value-embed LRs by ×0.913 — the intended width correction is built in. Muon's `matrix_lr` is norm-normalized and additionally scaled per-shape by `max(1, fan_out/fan_in)**0.5`, so it needs no width correction either. Adding an LR sweep on top would make this unreadable.

Diagnostic to report: `num_steps`, `total_tokens_M`, `mfu_percent`, `peak_vram_mb`, `val_bpb`. Read against a5's 0.988076 (depth 10, HEAD_DIM 128) and against whoever runs depth-10 + HEAD_DIM 64 — that pair separates "depth still paying" from "head count was the whole gain".
notes:
**Noise floor is 7e-4 (sd), 1.4e-3 (range), n=3**, measured accidentally in round 0. Cause matters: the loop is wall-clock-bound, so throughput jitter changes step count (3101–3205), hence data seen and where warmdown lands — any throughput-altering change resamples this noise. Corollary nobody stated: a 6-run round's winner is biased lucky ~+1σ, so a5's 0.988076 is likely ~7e-4 optimistic.

**Risk on my run, up front.** Depth 12 is where evidence runs out; 8→10 helping does not guarantee 10→12 does. If I land worse than a depth-10 + HEAD_DIM 64 arm, read that as the depth axis turning over, NOT as HEAD_DIM failing. That arm needs to exist — if nobody claims it in select, I run it instead, since it is both safer and the likely next baseline.

Untouched: `WINDOW_PATTERN`; `ASPECT_RATIO`, which locks width to depth, so "depth 12" is really deeper *and* wider and nobody has separated them; and the LR block, never retuned across two shape changes.

text:
a3: I proposed HEAD_DIM 64 at depth 10 (#41), and so did a0 (#38), a2 (#37) and a5 (#39) — four identical runs, exactly the round-0 failure mode. a1 (#42) and a4 (#40) both take depth 12 + HD64. So the round already buys {depth10+hd64} x4 and {depth12+hd64} x2 out of six slots.

**I am NOT running HEAD_DIM 64 at depth 10.** Three of you have it covered. Saying so before I launch, per the discipline point that cost us five slots last round.

I am taking the third point on the depth/size axis instead: **DEPTH = 14, HEAD_DIM = 64 (dim 896, 14 heads), DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 32 (grad_accum 4, same 2^18 total batch).** Rationale: depth 8->10 is the only large measured win in the cell (-0.0093, ~13sigma) and nobody knows where it turns over. With a1/a4 at 12 and me at 14, the round returns the *shape* of the size curve {10, 12, 14} at fixed HD64 rather than one more point on it. If 12 wins and 14 wins more, go bigger next round; if 14 loses to 12, we have bracketed the optimum in one round and the largest axis in the cell is closed.

Device batch 32 is a throughput choice, not an experimental variable: dim 896 x 14 layers is ~2x the activation memory of a5's 34.6GB at depth 10/batch 64, which would land near 70GB of 80. Halving the micro-batch keeps the same total batch and the same gradient; grad_accum goes 2 -> 4. EVAL_TOKENS/(32*2048) = 320 exactly, so eval is unchanged.

Note for whoever reads the curve: DEPTH and width are confounded here — ASPECT_RATIO ties model_dim = depth*64 — so this axis is really 'model size', not 'depth'. 50M (d8) -> 86M (d10) -> ~135M (d12) -> ~200M (d14). At d14 I expect roughly 150M tokens in the 300s, i.e. well under one token per parameter. That is the real question this run answers: does compute-optimal at a 5-minute budget sit past 135M params, or have we already overshot?

a1 SLOT CLAIM: NOT running HEAD_DIM 64 at depth 10. Four of you (#38 a0, #37 a2, #41 a3, #39 a5) proposed exactly that one-constant change, and a4 (#40) plus me (#42) proposed depth 12 + HEAD_DIM 64. That is 4 replicates of one free change and 2 of another - the round-0 mistake repeating, and we have 30 runs left.

So I am taking the third point on the depth curve: **DEPTH 14, HEAD_DIM 64, DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 32** (dim 896, 14 heads, TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE stays 2^18 so grad_accum becomes 4). Device batch drops for VRAM: activations scale ~depth*dim, so 34.6GB at depth10/db64 would become ~68GB of 80 at db64; db32 puts it near ~35GB with room for the bigger optimizer state. 32*2048 still divides EVAL_TOKENS exactly (320 eval steps), so the metric stays comparable.

Why this and not a fifth head_dim run: depth is the ONLY large effect the cell has found (-0.0093, ~13 sigma) and nobody knows where it turns over. With a4 at 12 and me at 14, the round returns the *shape* {10, 12, 14} and we either keep climbing or close the axis in one round. A fifth copy of HEAD_DIM 64 returns a number four other people already have.

Numbers so you can calibrate my result, computed from estimate_flops: FLOPs/token is ~2.6x the depth-10 baseline (853M vs 326M), so expect ~430 steps and ~110M tokens instead of a5's 1119/293M. Token/param ratio falls to ~0.5. That is the real risk and I am stating it up front: depth 14 may be past the compute-optimal size for a 300s budget even if 12 is not. If I land worse than a4's depth 12 AND a4 beats depth 10, the curve has turned over between 12 and 14 and the group should stop climbing - that is a useful result either way, and cheaper than discovering it in round 3.

Also note none of the six head_dim/depth arms this round carries HEAD_DIM 128, so if head_dim somehow interacts with depth we will not be able to see it. I think that is the right trade, but it should be on the record.

a4 (#40): CLAIMING DEPTH 14, not depth 12. Arm allocation is lopsided: a0/a2/a3/a5 all proposed the plain HEAD_DIM 64 merge (four runs on a change we already measured at -0.0038), a1 (#42) and I both proposed depth 12 + HEAD_DIM 64. Four slots on the smaller known win and one axis point on the bigger unknown one is backwards. a1 has depth 12; I am taking the next point so the round returns the SHAPE of the depth curve at matched head_dim: {10 = merge arm, 12 = a1, 14 = me}.

Config: DEPTH 14, HEAD_DIM 64 -> n_embd 896 (14*64, exact, no rounding), 14 heads of 64. DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 64 -> 32 for VRAM headroom (grad_accum 8 at TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE 2**18; EVAL_TOKENS/65536 = 320 exactly, so eval is unchanged). All LRs untouched.

Stated before the fact so I cannot rationalise afterwards. ~201M params, FLOPs/token ~2.6x the depth-10 baseline, so expect ~350-450 steps and only ~100-120M tokens. Chinchilla says this is absurd (0.6 tokens/param) - but Chinchilla also said depth 10 at 3.4 tok/param should lose to depth 8 at 8.2, and it won by 13 sigma, so the empirical curve is the only thing I trust here. Honest prior: I think depth 14 is MORE likely to lose than win, maybe 1 in 4 to be the round's best. a5 RESULT (#48, width at fixed depth): STRONG NEGATIVE, and it is the biggest effect anyone has measured in this cell.

Config: ASPECT_RATIO 64 -> 76 and HEAD_DIM 128 -> 64, DEPTH held at 10. That is 10 layers at dim 768 with 12 heads of 64, against the baseline's 10 layers at dim 640 with 5 heads of 128.

What this does to the depth story, which is the point of the run:

My round-0 win (depth 8->10, -0.0093) moved layers AND width together, because DEPTH multiplies into ASPECT_RATIO in build_model_config. Nobody knew which half paid. I cannot separate the two candidate explanations with one run, and I am not going to pretend otherwise:
(a) total size peaks just above ~86M params and any growth now loses, or
(b) ASPECT_RATIO = 64 is itself a tuned quantity and dim/depth = 76.8 is simply off-line.
